title: Prevent Emails from Being Sent to Specific Recipients and Domains
summary: Stop emails from being sent to specific recipients or domains with the new Recipient-Based DLP Block List.
body_text: Share Stop emails from being sent to specific recipients or domains with the new Recipient-Based DLP Block List. Organizations often need to prevent users from sending emails to specific external recipients or domains for compliance, security, or business reasons. Check Point Email Security now allows administrators to create Recipient-Based DLP Block Lists, providing a simple way to define recipients that should never receive emails from the organization. The new capability is available under Security Settings > Exceptions > DLP > Block List and allows administrators to create block list entries based on either individual recipient email addresses or entire recipient domains. When a user attempts to send an email to a blocked recipient, the message is automatically flagged as a DLP violation and the configured DLP workflow is triggered. This enhancement gives organizations greater control over outbound communications and helps reduce the risk of accidental data exposure, policy violations, or unauthorized information sharing. Whether the goal is to block communication with former partners, competitors, personal email domains, or specific individuals, administrators can now enforce these restrictions directly within Check Point Email Security using a centralized and easy-to-manage policy. This feature is gradually being deployed and will become available in customer portals over the next 7 days.

title: Anixa Biosciences Announces Presentations of Two Clinical-Stage Immunotherapy Programs at New York Academy of Sciences' Frontiers in Cancer Immunotherapy Symposium
body_text: Anixa Biosciences Announces Presentations of Two Clinical-Stage Immunotherapy Programs at New York Academy of Sciences' Frontiers in Cancer Immunotherapy Symposium Download as PDF June 11, 2026 Ovarian cancer CAR-T therapy, lira-cel, presentation to highlight positive survival observations from ongoing Phase 1 clinical trial Breast cancer vaccine presentation to include final Phase 1 data showing all major primary endpoints were met and protocol-defined immune responses in 74% of participants Presentations highlight Anixa's clinical progress and collaborations with leading cancer research institutions SAN JOSE, Calif. , June 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Anixa Biosciences, Inc. ("Anixa" or the "Company") (NASDAQ: ANIX), a biotechnology company focused on the treatment and prevention of cancer, today announced that two of its clinical-stage immunotherapy programs will be presented at the New York Academy of Sciences' Frontiers in Cancer Immunotherapy symposium, being held June 22 – 23, 2026, at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York City. The presentations will highlight Anixa's ovarian cancer CAR-T therapy, liraltagene autoleucel, or lira-cel, which is being evaluated in an ongoing Phase 1 clinical trial, and Anixa's breast cancer vaccine program, which completed a Phase 1 clinical trial in which all major primary endpoints were met and protocol-defined immune responses were generated in 74% of participants. Frontiers in Cancer Immunotherapy brings together leading researchers, clinicians and industry innovators to explore next-generation therapies that are transforming cancer treatment. The symposium will showcase research and emerging approaches in areas including cancer vaccines, bispecifics, modulation of the tumor microenvironment, AI-driven discovery of immunotherapy and cell-based therapies for solid tumors. Additionally, Dr. Stephen Schoenberger, PhD, a world-renowned immunologist at the La Jolla Institute for Immunology and a member of Anixa's Clinical Advisory Board, will be a featured speaker at the symposium. "Presenting both of our clinical-stage immunotherapy programs at this symposium is an important opportunity to highlight the progress of our pipeline and the strength of the collaborations supporting these programs," said Dr. Amit Kumar, PhD, Chairman and CEO of Anixa Biosciences. "Our ovarian cancer CAR-T therapy and breast cancer vaccine program are being advanced with leading clinical and scientific institutions, and we believe these presentations underscore the potential of Anixa's approach to treating and preventing cancer." The Company's lira-cel presentation, titled "A Phase I Clinical Trial of an Infusion of Autologous T cells Genetically Engineered with a Chimeric Receptor to Target the Follicle-Stimulating Hormone Receptor in Patients with Recurrent Ovarian Cancer," will be given by Dr. Pamela D. Garzone, PhD, Chief Development Officer of Anixa Biosciences. The presentation will report the clinical trial design and objectives, as well as the current status of Anixa's ongoing Phase 1 clinical trial of lira-cel. The lira-cel presentation reflects contributions from investigators and collaborators across Anixa, Moffitt Cancer Center, Roswell Park Cancer Center, the University of Chicago School of Medicine and Duke University Medical Center. Project team members cited on the poster include: Dr. Marco L. Davila, MD, PhD (Department of Medicine, Roswell Park Cancer Center) Dr. Daniel Abate-Daga, PhD (Department of Immunology, Moffitt Cancer Center) Dr. Melissa McGettigan, MD (Department of Radiology, Moffitt Cancer Center) Dr. Xuefeng Wang, PhD (Department of Biostatistics and Bioinformatics, Moffitt Cancer Center) Dr. Theresa Boyle, MD, PhD (Department of Pathology, Moffitt Cancer Center) Dr. Amit Kumar, PhD (Anixa Biosciences, Inc.) Denise Dorman, RN (Department of Gynecologic Oncology, Moffitt Cancer Center) Dr. Richard Koya, MD, PhD (University of Chicago School of Medicine) Dr. Christopher Cubitt, PhD (Immune Monitoring Core, Moffitt Cancer Center) Dr. Jose Conejo-Garcia, MD, PhD (Department of Immunology, Duke University Medical Center) Dr. Robert M. Wenham, MD, MS (Principal Investigator, Department of Gynecologic Oncology, Moffitt Cancer Center) The Company's breast cancer vaccine presentation, titled "Phase I Trial of an Alpha-Lactalbumin (aLA) Vaccine for Breast Cancer," will be given by Dr. Emily Esakov Rhoades, PhD, FDA/IND Trial Program Manager, Cleveland Clinic Cancer Institute. The presentation will report final Phase 1 findings for the investigational vaccine, including that all major primary endpoints were met, the vaccine was safe and well tolerated at the maximum tolerated dose based on safety and tolerability, and protocol-defined immune responses were elicited in 74% of trial participants. Immunohistochemistry of tumor samples demonstrating alpha-lactalbumin expression will also be reported. The breast cancer vaccine presentation reflects contributions from Cleveland Clinic clinicians, translational researchers, patient advocates, and collaborators involved in advancing the program. The Cleveland Clinic team includes: Dr. Justin M. Johnson, PhD (Department of Inflammation & Immunity, Cleveland Clinic) Holly B. Levengood (Department of Inflammation & Immunity, Cleveland Clinic Cancer Institute) Dr. Azka Ali, MD (Cleveland Clinic Cancer Institute) Dr. Hannah Gilmore, MD (Robert J. Tomsich Pathology and Laboratory Medicine Institute) Dr. Megan L. Kruse, MD (Cleveland Clinic Cancer Institute) Dr. Erin E. Roesch, MD (Cleveland Clinic Cancer Institute) Dr. Tiffany Onger, MD (Cleveland Clinic Cancer Institute) Brenna Elliott (Cleveland Clinic Cancer Institute) Elena Haury (Cleveland Clinic Cancer Institute) Carolyn Porvasnik (Cleveland Clinic Cancer Institute) Tobey Young (Previvorsandsurvivors.com, Inc.) Terri Coutee (DiepCJourney Foundation) Judith A. Fitzgerald, BCPA (Sisters4Prevention) Dr. Thaddeus S. Stappenbeck, MD, PhD (Co-Principal Investigator, Chair – Department of Inflammation & Immunity, Cleveland Clinic) Dr. G. Thomas Budd, MD (Principal Investigator, Cleveland Clinic Cancer Institute) About Lira-cel, Anixa's CAR-T Therapy for Recurrent Ovarian Cancer Liraltagene autoleucel, or lira-cel, uniquely targets the follicle-stimulating hormone receptor (FSHR), which is selectively expressed on ovarian and testis cells, tumor vasculature, and certain cancer cells, but not in other healthy tissue. The ongoing Phase 1 trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05316129) is enrolling adult women with recurrent ovarian cancer who are platinum resistant and have progressed after at least two prior therapies. About Anixa's Breast Cancer Vaccine Anixa's breast cancer vaccine represents a novel approach to the prevention and treatment of breast cancer. The vaccine is based on immunizing against human α-lactalbumin, a protein associated with lactation that is highly expressed in certain types of breast cancer. This "retired" protein vaccine strategy aims to selectively prime the immune system to prevent tumor formation while avoiding harm to normal tissue. About Anixa Biosciences, Inc. Anixa is a clinical-stage biotechnology company focused on the treatment and prevention of cancer. Anixa's therapeutic portfolio consists of liraltagene autoleucel, or lira-cel, an ovarian cancer immunotherapy being developed in collaboration with Moffitt Cancer Center, which uses a novel type of CAR-T, known as chimeric endocrine receptor-T cell (CER-T) technology. This technology is differentiated from other cell therapies as the natural ligand of the FSHR receptor, FSH, binds to the FSHR receptor on the tumor cell instead of an antibody fragment. Moffitt is a world leader in cancer immunotherapy treatments, pioneering next-generation cell therapies such as CAR-T, and tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) to harness the power of the immune system. The Company's vaccine portfolio includes vaccines being developed in collaboration with Cleveland Clinic to treat and prevent breast cancer and ovarian cancer, as well as additional cancer vaccines to address many intractable cancers, including high incidence malignancies in lung, colon, and prostate. These vaccine technologies focus on immunizing against "retired" proteins that have been found to be expressed in certain forms of cancer. The breast and ovarian cancer vaccines were developed at Cleveland Clinic and exclusively licensed to Anixa. body_text: Nicole Parisi Vignesh Palaniappan Finding the right information across dashboards, monitors, and telemetry sources takes time, even for experienced engineers. title: Cosmic Rundown: Deno Desktop, Zig Funding, and the Claude Thinking Debate
summary: Deno ships native desktop app support. Mitchell Hashimoto pledges $400k more to Zig. A blog post questions whether Claude's extended thinking shows real reasoning. Plus open model momentum and a Codex logging bug.
body_text: Deno Desktop Arrives Deno has released Deno Desktop , enabling developers to build native desktop applications using TypeScript and web technologies. The feature uses system webviews rather than bundling Chromium, resulting in significantly smaller binaries than Electron alternatives. The Hacker News discussion covers the tradeoffs. Smaller bundle sizes and native performance are clear wins. The inconsistency of system webviews across platforms is the familiar counterargument. For teams already invested in the Deno ecosystem, this removes a significant gap in what the runtime can target. For content-driven applications, the combination of Deno's TypeScript-first approach and native desktop support opens possibilities for local-first CMS editors, offline content tools, and hybrid applications that sync with cloud APIs. $400k More for Zig Mitchell Hashimoto, co-founder of HashiCorp, has pledged another $400,000 to the Zig Software Foundation . This follows his previous donations and reflects continued confidence in Zig as systems programming infrastructure. The discussion explores what sustainable open source funding looks like when it depends on individual benefactors rather than corporate sponsors or foundations. Zig's approach of maintaining independence while accepting large donations is working so far, though questions about long-term sustainability remain. For teams building performance-critical infrastructure, Zig continues to mature as an alternative to C and C++ with better ergonomics and safety guarantees. Is Claude's Extended Thinking Authentic? A technical analysis titled "Claude Code's extended thinking is a summary, not authentic thinking" argues that the visible reasoning shown in Claude Code's extended thinking mode is a post-hoc summary rather than the actual inference process. The Hacker News thread debates whether this distinction matters practically. Some argue that transparent summaries are more useful than raw token streams anyway. Others see it as a transparency issue: if users believe they are watching the model "think," showing a reconstruction instead is misleading. This connects to broader questions about AI observability. When AI agents generate content or make decisions, understanding how they arrived at outputs matters for debugging, trust, and improvement. Whether you see the actual process or a summary of it changes what you can learn. Open Models Gain Ground A post titled "There is minimal downside to switching to open models" makes the case that open-weight models have reached practical parity with proprietary alternatives for many use cases. The discussion adds nuance. Open models excel at tasks where you need full control, local deployment, or custom fine-tuning. Proprietary models still lead on certain benchmarks and offer managed infrastructure. The practical question is which tradeoffs matter for your specific workflow. For content operations, this matters because model choice affects cost, latency, privacy, and customization options. A headless CMS with AI capabilities needs to support multiple model backends as the landscape continues shifting. Codex Logging Bug Fills SSDs A GitHub issue reports that OpenAI's Codex can write terabytes of logs to local storage under certain conditions, potentially filling developer SSDs. The thread documents the debugging process and workarounds. The broader lesson is that AI coding tools introduce new categories of resource consumption that traditional development environments did not anticipate. Monitoring disk usage, token consumption, and API costs becomes part of the development workflow. Quick Hits Facial recognition resistance : Never Give Them Your Face provides resources for understanding and limiting facial recognition exposure. The discussion covers practical countermeasures and policy implications. NSF funding shifts : The National Science Foundation is slashing basic research to fund tech initiatives . The thread debates short-term application focus versus long-term foundational research. Efficient image inpainting : Moebius is a 0.2B parameter model that achieves 10B-level performance on image inpainting tasks. The discussion covers the architectural innovations enabling this efficiency. Prompt injection theory : A new paper presents a theory of why prompt injection works . Understanding the mechanics helps build more robust AI systems. Wind-powered shipping : DHL is partnering on wind-powered cargo ships for sustainable logistics. The thread examines the economics and scalability. What This Means for Content Teams Deno Desktop matters if you are building content tools that need to work offline or require native performance. The smaller binary sizes compared to Electron make distribution more practical for utility applications. The Claude thinking transparency debate connects directly to AI content workflows. When an agent writes or edits content, understanding its reasoning helps you improve prompts, catch errors, and build trust with stakeholders. Whether you see actual inference or summaries, the key is having some visibility into the process. The open models discussion affects vendor strategy. Teams building on AI-powered content platforms should consider whether their CMS supports multiple model backends or locks them into a single provider. Flexibility here becomes more valuable as the model landscape evolves. Building content infrastructure that needs AI flexibility and native integrations? title: Industrial Thermal Imaging Camera Specifications Checklist
summary: Industrial thermal imaging camera specifications explained: a plant manager's procurement checklist for resolution, sensitivity, range, and supplier fit.
body_text: Choosing the right industrial thermal camera comes down to a short list of specifications and an even shorter list of supplier questions, and getting both right is what separates early fault detection from unplanned downtime. Resolution and thermal sensitivity (NETD) decide how small a problem you can catch and how early you catch it. Spectral band and temperature range have to match your actual equipment, not a generic data sheet. Integration, environmental rating, and calibration determine whether the camera survives your plant floor and feeds your monitoring system. Supplier depth and supply-chain stability matter as much as any number on the spec sheet for a multi-year program. Build your requirements around the application first, then pressure-test every vendor against the same checklist. Specifying a thermal monitoring system used to be something you could hand off and forget. That changed the moment infrared inspection became an enforceable maintenance standard for electrical equipment under NFPA 70B in 2023. Reading industrial thermal imaging camera specifications correctly is the difference between catching a failing bearing weeks early and writing up another emergency work order. This guide is a working procurement checklist. It covers the handful of specifications that actually matter for industrial monitoring, the trade-offs hiding behind each one, and the supplier questions that rarely make it onto a requisition form but should. By the end, the plant manager or reliability engineer should be able to write a requirement set that you can defend in a budget review. What Do Industrial Thermal Imaging Camera Specifications Actually Tell You? A thermal camera converts the infrared energy radiating off your equipment into a temperature image. The specifications are simply the language vendors use to describe how well it does that job in your environment. Read them as performance promises tied to your application, not as a scoreboard where the biggest number wins. Demand for these systems is climbing. The thermal imaging market was valued at about $4.5 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach $7.66 billion by 2031 , driven heavily by industrial inspection and predictive maintenance. Having more options on the market is good news for your budget and bad news for clarity because spec sheets aren't standardized, and vendors emphasize whatever makes their product look strongest. The smartest move is to define your application before you compare a single model. What is the smallest fault you need to detect, at what working distance, across what temperature range, in what conditions? Once you can answer that, industrial thermal imaging camera specifications stop being abstract and start telling you exactly which system fits. Our industrial thermal imaging resources go deeper on application matching if you want a reference while you build requirements. Which Specs Belong on Your Thermal Camera Procurement Checklist? Six specifications carry most of the weight for industrial monitoring. Get these industrial thermal camera specs right, and you can cut through almost any data sheet. Here's the quick reference, followed by the why behind each. Specification What to look for (industrial monitoring) What it affects Resolution 320×240 minimum; 640×512 for small targets or longer distances How small a fault you can resolve Thermal sensitivity (NETD) 30 to 60 mK for uncooled systems; lower is more sensitive How early subtle heat anomalies appear Spectral band LWIR (8 to 14 µm) for most plant monitoring; MWIR (3 to 5 µm) for high-temperature processes Suitability for your equipment and environment Temperature range Matched to your hottest and coldest assets Whether readings stay accurate across your equipment Environmental rating Sealed enclosure rated for dust, washdown, and vibration Reliability on a working plant floor Integration GigE Vision, Modbus TCP, ONVIF, or your SCADA and CMMS protocol Whether the data reaches your monitoring system Resolution and Detector Sensitivity Resolution is the pixel count on the detector, and it sets how much detail you capture. For general panel and motor scanning, 320×240 is a reasonable floor. When you need to resolve a single overheating lug or inspect from a safe distance, 640×512 earns its cost. Don't buy more pixels than your working distance and target size require because higher resolution quickly drives up the price. Thermal sensitivity, measured as Noise Equivalent Temperature Difference (NETD), is the spec that decides how early you catch problems. A lower NETD means the camera resolves finer temperature differences, so a connection that's only slightly warm shows up before it becomes a fire risk. For uncooled industrial systems, look for NETD in the 30–60 mK range, and treat lower numbers as a genuine advantage for early fault detection. Our guide on how to choose an industrial thermal imaging camera breaks the resolution and NETD trade-off down further. Spectral Band and Temperature Range Most plant monitoring lives in the long-wave infrared band, LWIR (8–14 µm), which handles electrical panels, rotating equipment, and process monitoring well in a compact, low-maintenance package. Very high-temperature processes, such as furnaces and molten metal, can call for MWIR (3–5 µm) instead. The right band depends on what you're watching, so confirm it against your hottest assets rather than defaulting to whatever a vendor stocks. Temperature measurement range matters just as much. A camera tuned for a comfortable office wall will saturate on a 400-degree process line. Match the range to both your coldest and hottest equipment, and check that accuracy holds across that span, not just at a single calibration point. Optics, Field of View, and Environment The lens defines field of view and how many pixels land on your target at a given distance. A strong detector paired with the wrong lens still produces a thermal image that lacks enough pixels on the feature you care about, so specify optics around your real working distance. A wide field of view quickly scans large areas, while a narrower one puts more detail on distant targets. Finally, the camera has to survive where it lives. A working plant brings dust, vibration, washdown, and temperature swings, so an appropriately sealed and rated enclosure is not optional. Thermal imaging performs well in low-visibility conditions, such as darkness, smoke, and dust, which is part of why it suits industrial settings. Heavy rain and direct high-radiance sources remain limitations worth noting in any outdoor application. The Industrial Thermal Imaging Camera Specifications Checklist Use this list as your procurement worksheet. Each line is something to confirm in writing before a purchase order goes out, and together they keep a thermal camera procurement decision honest. Run every candidate through the same plant manager thermal camera checklist so your comparisons stay consistent. Confirm resolution against your smallest target. Verify the pixel count resolves your smallest expected fault at your typical inspection distance, not just in a vendor demo. Set an NETD ceiling. Require thermal sensitivity in the 30–60 mK range for uncooled systems, and favor lower values where early detection drives the program. Lock in the spectral band. Specify LWIR (8–14 µm) for standard monitoring or MWIR (3–5 µm) for high-temperature processes, based on your equipment. Define the temperature range and accuracy. Match it to your hottest and coldest assets and require accuracy to hold across the full span. Specify optics and field of view. Tie the lens choice to your working distance so that enough pixels land on the target. Require an environmental rating. Demand a sealed enclosure rated for your plant's dust, vibration, and washdown conditions. Verify integration paths. Confirm support for your SCADA, CMMS, or PLC protocols (GigE Vision, Modbus TCP, ONVIF, or an open API) before purchase. Check export-control exposure. Note that systems running faster than 9 Hz frame rates can trigger ITAR or EAR considerations, which affect sourcing and documentation. Pin down calibration and reporting. Require defined calibration intervals, emissivity controls, and reporting tools that support NFPA 70B documentation and audits. Evaluate supplier depth. Assess engineering support, lifecycle commitment, and supply-chain stability, which we cover in the next section. How Should a Plant Manager Weigh Specs Against Supplier Fit? A perfect spec sheet from a fragile supplier is a liability. For a system you expect to run for years, the people behind the camera matter as much as the industrial thermal camera specs printed on the data sheet. Three supplier factors deserve real weight in any plant manager's thermal camera decision. Supply continuity comes first because a component change or discontinued line mid-program can stall your monitoring system entirely. Engineering support comes second, since the gap between a functional install and a high-performing one usually closes during integration, not before the order. Compliance comes third, covering both export controls and documentation that holds up in an NFPA 70B audit. The savings on the line are not small. The U.S. Department of Energy's Federal Energy Management Program attributes roughly 8–12% maintenance-cost savings to predictive maintenance over preventive programs and considerably more against purely reactive approaches. A reliable supplier protects those returns over the life of the program. For sourcing strategy specifically, our piece on strengthening your infrared optics supply chain is worth a read, and the predictive maintenance thermal imaging guide ties specs back to program outcomes. Here is how a purpose-built commercial-grade system compares to a basic general-purpose camera on the criteria that affect industrial programs: Consideration Commercial-grade industrial system Basic general-purpose camera Operation Built for continuous, embedded duty Designed for intermittent handheld use Sensitivity (NETD) Typically 30 to 50 mK Often 60 mK or higher Integration Industrial protocols and open APIs Limited or proprietary outputs Support Application engineering and lifecycle support Minimal customization or guidance Supply continuity Sourced for multi-year program stability Subject to product-line changes Neither tier is wrong. A general-purpose camera is fine for occasional spot checks. For a monitoring program your operations depend on, the commercial-grade path almost always pays for itself in reliability and support. FAQ: Industrial Thermal Imaging Camera Specifications What resolution do I need for an industrial thermal camera? For most panel, motor, and process scanning, 320×240 is a sensible minimum. Step up to 640×512 when you need to resolve small components or inspect from longer distances. Match resolution to your target size and working distance rather than buying the highest count available, since extra pixels add cost you may not use. What NETD is good enough for predictive maintenance? For uncooled industrial systems, NETD in the 30–60 mK range is the working standard, and lower values within that band detect subtle anomalies earlier. Early detection is the entire point of predictive maintenance, so sensitivity is one spec where paying for better performance usually pays back. Is LWIR or MWIR better for plant monitoring? LWIR (8–14 µm) covers most industrial monitoring, including electrical, mechanical, and general process work in a compact and low-maintenance form. MWIR (3–5 µm) suits specialized high-temperature applications, such as furnace and molten-metal monitoring. Choose the band based on your equipment and temperatures, not on which one a vendor happens to stock. Can a thermal camera measure accurately through an inspection window? Yes, as long as you account for the window's infrared transmission and apply a consistent correction. Keep comparisons window-to-window, expect a small signal penalty, and document your settings so readings stay comparable over time. How do I keep a procurement decision from being just a spec comparison? Define your application first, then hold every vendor to the same checklist, including the supplier-fit criteria. Two cameras with identical specs can deliver very different results once supply continuity, engineering support, and integration enter the picture, so weight those alongside the numbers. Ready to Specify a System You Can Stand Behind? A good procurement decision is mostly preparation. Define the application, set your specifications around it, and pressure-test both the camera and the company behind it against a single consistent checklist. Do that, and you turn a complicated purchase into a defensible one. Download the procurement checklist above and bring it to your next vendor conversation. When supplier fit becomes the deciding factor, it helps to work with a partner who controls the full chain from optical materials through finished camera assemblies. title: Companies have claimed they can read documents for years, but has the problem been solved?
summary: Why context and audit agents will be the right solutions to reading documents
body_text: Companies have claimed they can read documents for years, but has the problem been solved? Why context and audit agents will be the right solutions to reading documents AI for Actuaries @Tesora.ai , Philo Bishay , and Vivek Jun 05, 2026 First, it was called OCR. Then data capture, intelligent document processing, extraction, and now companies call it ingestion (with ETL still penciled into a deck somewhere). No problem in software has been renamed this many times, and with each iteration arrives with a fresh wave of companies promising it is solved. Our contrarian thesis is that, as of this year, it finally is. YC-backed providers like Reducto and Extend, the frontier models underneath them (Gemini, OpenAI, Anthropic), and vertical players like ProSights now read a clean page as well as a careful person, and a thousand pages costs about a coffee. A Luckin coffee, not Starbucks : Gemini Flash reads six thousand pages for a dollar. On clean text, the engines passed 99% years ago. On OmniDocBench’s tables the same models drop to the mid-eighties, which is the number a loss run actually tests: Insurance documents are rarely clean. Which is why it caught us off guard that the better these tools got, the less comfortable insurance has been at putting one in front of their own loss runs. This explains a habit we see in every customer. Before a chief actuary asks how our agent reasons or what it does with a rate filing, they ask whether it can read their submissions accurately, the way a surgeon might open with a question about the scalpel. They have been burned before, and have learned that ingestion is the one question that predicts whether anything built on top of it can be trusted ( garbage in, garbage out…) Ninety-seven percent is the wrong number to celebrate Insurance does not get to use the accuracy that satisfies everyone else. Ninety-seven percent is about where the best extractors land on messy documents, and for a consumer app misreading three receipts in a hundred that is a strong grade. The same figure is also a three percent failure rate, and in insurance those three errors are not spread evenly across fields you can afford to lose. Each square is one extracted value. A 97% benchmark score leaves 3 wrong in 100. In insurance the errors are not random typos, they are the development factor, the netgross flag, the valuation date. Any one is the loss pick. Illustrative. On a loss run, which often arrives as a scanned fax of a printout, the value the model fumbles is as likely to be the development factor, the net-versus-gross flag, or the valuation date as anything harmless, and any one of those is the number the indication turns on. A wrong word in a chatbot is a sentence you laugh off. But a wrong number in a rate filing is a meeting with a regulator three years later, in front of a file note that reads “rolled forward from prior.” They are expensive because they are hardly reading errors at all. “Incurred loss” can mean paid losses plus case reserves as of a valuation date, or it can mean ultimate losses carrying a provision for claims not yet reported, and on an immature accident year those two numbers live in different area codes. A general extractor transcribes both columns flawlessly and cannot tell that it has blended them, because the carrier labeled them with the same word. Nor is the trouble confined to paper: Philo recently sent over a voice memo of edits, we ran it through a leading transcription model, and it turned his actuarial shorthand into confident gibberish. Telling it to think like an actuary only produced a second answer, equally confident and equally wrong. The better the model reads, the better it hides its mistakes Start with autocorrect. It is right so often that you stop proofreading, and then one day it changes “festival” to “funeral” and the message goes out anyway. The tool did not get worse. You got comfortable, and it saved its one mistake for the moment you had stopped looking. Document models do the same thing, in two ways at once. As they get more accurate they clear the easy errors first, so the mistakes left over are the hard, judgment-heavy ones, which in insurance are also the costly ones. You get fewer errors, but a bigger share of the ones that remain land on a number that matters. At the same time, the better the model reads, the more people trust it and the less they check. Not even actuaries are immune: a team that will re-run a triangle which is already balanced will, after a tool has been right all quarter, quietly stop re-running anything. Put simply, a better model fails less often, but when it does fail the mistake is both more important and less likely to be caught. That is why the benchmark score and the real risk pull apart. The leaderboard number keeps climbing, while the thing you actually care about, an expensive error slipping into a signed filing, can sit still or quietly get worse. The fix is introducing doubt, not assuming accuracy in the first go The answer is not a sharper set of eyes but a system that refuses to take a confident reading at face value. It checks each value against the structure of the document and the carrier’s history, so an ambiguous “incurred” column is resolved against what the rest of the exhibit implies rather than guessed. That is grounding rather than roleplay, the thing no instruction to think like an actuary can stand in for. We call these “audit” agents within a harness. Text-capture and table-structure bars are directionally consistent with public OCR/extraction benchmarks. “Actuarial field meaning” (correct reading of incurred vs paid, valuation date, ALAE bundling) is Tesora internal evaluation, shown to illustrate the argument. Tesora pairs Claude Opus 4.8 with a harness trained for actuarial work. The behavior that earns the signature, though, is the one no benchmark rewards and every careful actuary already practices: knowing when to stop. When a value falls outside the range the system has earned the right to be sure about, it abstains and hands that value to a person rather than emit a number as certain-looking as the rest. That reverses the complacency instead of feeding it, and tells the reviewer which cells to distrust. Higher accuracy improves the average. Calibrated doubt surfaces the expensive mistake, and in a regulated workflow that is the entire game. The labs are unlikely to build this, because the data that would teach these distinctions sits inside carriers who have every reason to keep it there. From the outside, ingestion will keep looking finished. Inside insurance, the work that is left is not teaching the machine to read more of the page correctly. It is teaching it to admit which parts it might have read wrong, and to say so before an actuary signs underneath. Tesora builds AI agents and workflows that understand actuaries. If an ~extracted~ loss run has ever lied to you, we would like to hear from you. title: Presource® Solutions helps hospitals drive efficiencies, easing burdens on providers
summary: Perioperative nurses are no strangers to a hectic workday. As critical members of a surgical team, they are responsible for a great deal of work prior to, during and after a patient procedure....
body_text: Perioperative nurses are no strangers to a hectic workday. As critical members of a surgical team, they are responsible for a great deal of work prior to, during and after a patient procedure. This includes everything from setting up the operating room to assisting during the procedure and cleaning up afterwards. Their preparation is a major part of any procedure. The right instruments and supplies must be selected from storage rooms, individually logged in hospital records and properly set up for the surgical team. Each item represents additional time during setup, which can compound across the multiple procedures conducted daily, and that’s time away from direct care with patients. As facilities face mounting pressures to improve workflows and find cost savings, inefficiencies can seem particularly complex puzzles to solve. In an industry where time often equates to cost, driving product standardization and enhancing inventory management can help address these challenges. Building efficiency through kitting Cardinal Health™ Presource® Solutions is designed to support hospitals in pursuing operational efficiencies, easing burdens on busy providers. The business is staffed with clinicians and consultants who support clinicians with medical supply and surgical instrument kitting expertise. Through kits, also known as packs, Presource® Solutions helps create more efficient surgical workflows. Presource® Solutions offers standard packs, with the core components needed for common surgical procedures, and custom packs, meticulously designed to meet providers’ specific needs and preferences. For example, a standard pack for a minimally-invasive laparoscopy contains all required supplies, including adhesive bandages, a table cover, surgical blade, needles and syringes, drapes and gowns, sponges and towels and more, bundled together, sterilized and ready for use. Custom packs allow for specific clinical preferences or needs that may be in addition to supplies found in a standard procedural pack. An effectively designed kitting program means that nurses can grab one pack from inventory rather than pulling multiple items from various locations. This streamlined process can help simplify procedural setup and support supply consistency across procedures — which may help support clinician workflow and preparation. “When clinical staff spend less time in the storage room and more time providing patient care, everyone wins,” said Joe Gilles, Global Vice President of Marketing, Presource® Solutions. “Facilities are able to take on more procedures and providers can better focus on the needs of their patients.” Presource® Solutions clinical consultants work directly with hospitals and healthcare facilities to evaluate their supply needs across all patient procedures. Our consultants recommend the right mix of components based on procedural needs and ultimately establish a pack program that supports onsite efficiencies and helps streamline clinician workflows. Because procedural needs are constantly evolving, pack programs should too. The Presource® Solutions team provides regular program pack reviews to reassess how components are being used and whether staff preferences and procedure volumes have changed. During these reviews, our consultants meet with clinicians either virtually or in-person and create or adjust packs, equipping clinicians with exactly what they need for each procedure. The team also eliminates non-value products to help reduce expenses and waste. Facilities can save an average of $25,000 annually from custom pack reviews alone, depending on the facility’s size, program and agreement.1 Pack reviews can also help support health systems’ sustainability goals. Our team uses data-driven tools to show providers greenhouse gas emissions in optimized kits, identify opportunities to eliminate packaging waste and reduce the number of unused items that would otherwise enter the waste stream. On average, Presource® Solutions custom packs can result in more than 2,000 pounds of waste reduction per hospital per year , according to our Fiscal 2025 Sustainable Business Report. A closer look at clinical workflows In some cases, a healthcare facility’s path to streamlined surgical preparation might be hampered by the facility itself. If its physical layout isn’t conducive to efficiency, that may negate the potential benefits from a pack program. Our Presource® Solutions team includes logistical consulting to help determine how to best use available storage space. Primary logistics consultant Scott Wall, BA, BSN, MSN, works closely with clinical staff to review supply chain processes and efficiencies. Alongside our clinical and business consultants, Presource® Solutions logistics consulting can further enhance the benefits of a pack program by helping optimize storage and workflow processes. “Space is a common problem throughout hospitals and surgery centers,” said Wall. “Many hospitals want to scale pack programs across more procedures, but they don’t know how to store them. We can help them use their facility properly and plan for growth in the future.” Wall leverages deep expertise honed over decades of experience in surgical nursing and nursing administration, including service as a nurse in the Army National Guard and the Utah Air National Guard. He was first exposed to the power of logistics when working at a field hospital during a wartime deployment. This experience, as well as serving on humanitarian missions with the Utah Air National Guard, inspired him to specialize in healthcare logistics. “Our goal is to bring the clinical and materials minds together, balancing the operational needs of the hospital with clinical imperatives,” said Wall. “When I approach a program review, I often think about the patient laying on the surgical table. I’ve been that patient — I want to do what I can to be sure they can receive the best care possible.” Increasing efficiency at South Shore Hospital To highlight the benefits of optimizing procedural supply management, Wall shared how he stepped in to support South Shore Hospital Center for Orthopedics, Spine and Sports Medicine in Hingham, Massachusetts, whose leaders had determined that existing inventory management practices weren’t keeping pace with increasing procedural needs. According to Wall, South Shore converted an operating room into a storage room to address its lack of space for necessary supplies. Though this was intended to be temporary, the solution lasted longer than planned and limited the overall volume of surgical procedures the hospital could take on. Additionally, the operating room was located on the opposite side of the facility from other storage rooms, requiring clinical teams to walk all the way across the facility each time they needed to gather supplies for a procedure. This inefficient setup cut into time nurses could be spending with patients. “Presource® Solutions pack programs are an efficient, effective way to deliver surgical products,” said Wall. “But if your storage setup isn’t optimized, you could still be wasting time during procedural prep.” Ultimately, Wall recommended renovating the original storage space to create a better flow. The Presource® Solutions team collaborated with hospital stakeholders and an architecture group to help bring the renovation to life, crafted a revised pack program and worked closely with clinical staff to ensure the packs were stored effectively in the new layout. The updates allowed South Shore’s clinical staff to gain back critical time in their day, strengthen their workflows and increase bandwidth for direct patient care. In addition, Kathryn Rogers, Manager, PeriOp Supply Chain, South Shore Hospital, estimates the team’s accuracy when picking supplies for each procedure has increased to over 95%. “The layout and organization of the storage room provides ease in the ability to locate items for the clinical staff and case pick,” Rogers said. “It’s also decreased the time it takes to complete product ordering and put away surgical supplies and instruments.” More than a simple renovation, the project represented a total transformation of how South Shore Hospital Center for Orthopedics, Spine, and Sports Medicine approaches surgical preparation. “By streamlining through packs and smart logistics, we can support operational efficiency, room turnover and staff satisfaction,” said Wall. “We want to help your surgical staff be just as efficient outside the OR as they are in it.” Editor’s note: For more than 40 years, Presource ® Solutions has supported healthcare systems with inventory management and kitting solutions. Today, the business serves more than 4,000 healthcare customers across the U.S. You can learn more about the business here . 1: Cardinal Health data on file: Business & Clinical Optimization Metrics, June 1, 2026

body_text: Nearly half of individuals diagnosed with PTSD also meet criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD), making comorbid depression one of the most common and clinically significant complications of PTSD ~83.5% of patients with comorbid PTSD and MDD experienced a response (reduction in PTSD symptoms of ≥50%) following Deep TMS, with a mean reduction of 52% Results presented at a recent leading industry conference BURLINGTON, Mass. and JERUSALEM, June 29, 2026 — BrainsWay Ltd. (NASDAQ & TASE: BWAY) (“BrainsWay” or the “Company”), a global leader in advanced noninvasive brain stimulation technologies, today announced the presentation of positive new real-world data demonstrating significant improvements in patients with comorbid post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) treated with Deep Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (Deep TMS™). The findings were recently presented in a poster, titled “Safety and Efficacy of Deep TMS in Comorbid MDD and PTSD: Real-World Data Analysis,” by Colleen Hanlon, PhD, Vice President of Medical Affairs for BrainsWay, at a recent leading industry conference. This real-world data collection study evaluated the efficacy of Deep TMS as a tool to improve both PTSD and MDD symptoms in patients with comorbid disease. All 462 patients in the retrospective study, from 11 clinical sites, were diagnosed with both MDD and PTSD, received at least 20 Deep TMS treatment sessions using BrainsWay’s H1 or H7 coils. Outcomes included changes in the PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) and the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) before and after treatment. Of these patients, 83.5% experienced a response (a reduction in PTSD symptoms of ≥50%), with an average 52% reduction in PCL-5 scores. Patients also experienced substantial improvements in depression symptoms, including a 66.6% response rate (a reduction in depression symptoms of ≥50%), a 27.3% remission rate, and an average 50% reduction in PHQ-9 scores. Figure 1 Caption: Analysis of data demonstrate significant improvements in patients with comorbid post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) treated with Deep Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (Deep TMS™). “This study represents the largest real-world analysis of Deep TMS in patients with comorbid PTSD and major depressive disorder to date,” said Colleen Hanlon, Ph.D., Vice President of Medical Affairs at BrainsWay. “Given the significant burden associated with these co-occurring conditions, it is encouraging to see meaningful improvements in both PTSD and depression symptoms across a large and diverse patient population. These findings further strengthen the growing body of evidence supporting Deep TMS in complex psychiatric disorders.” “Patients living with both PTSD and depression often experience more severe symptoms and fewer effective treatment options,” said Toby Marton, M.D., Chief Medical Officer at Mindful Health and a lead contributor to this study. “The promising outcomes observed across multiple clinical sites highlight the potential of Deep TMS to deliver meaningful benefits and support its role as potential treatment option for this challenging patient population.” Deep TMS is not currently cleared by the FDA for the treatment of PTSD and/or comorbid PTSD and MDD, and the preliminary findings from the real-world study remain subject to peer review analysis. BrainsWay continues to lead the field with its proprietary H-coil technology, robust clinical research, and ongoing collaboration with providers and policymakers to expand access to care and improve the lives of patients. About BrainsWay BrainsWay is a global leader in advanced noninvasive neurostimulation treatments for mental health disorders. The Company is boldly advancing neuroscience with its proprietary Deep Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (Deep TMS™) platform technology to improve health and transform lives. BrainsWay is the first and only TMS company to obtain three FDA-cleared indications backed by pivotal clinical studies demonstrating clinically proven efficacy. Current indications include major depressive disorder (including reduction of anxiety symptoms, commonly referred to as anxious depression), obsessive-compulsive disorder, and smoking addiction. The Company is dedicated to leading through superior science and building on its unparalleled body of clinical evidence. Additional clinical trials of Deep TMS in various psychiatric, neurological, and addiction disorders are underway.
